case_name: Frontenac Children's Aid Society v. C. N.
text:
COURT FILE NO.:
Kingston
342/05

DATE:
March 29,
2007

SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE – FAMILY COURT

INFORMATION CONTAINED HEREIN IS PROHIBITED FROM
PUBLICATION PURSUANT TO SECTION 45(8) OF THE CHILD AND FAMILY SERVICES ACT

IN THE MATTER OF THE CHILD AND FAMILY SERVICES ACT,
R.S.O. 1990, c. C. 11
and in the matter of the children, T. N. born March
5, 1991 and C. N. born May 29, 1993

RE:
Frontenac Children’s Aid Society
v. C. N. (mother)

BEFORE:
The Honourable Madam Justice C. J.
Robertson

HEARD:
March 9, 2007

COUNSEL:
T.
Barnes, for the Applicant Society

Respondent/Mother,
not appearing, although properly served

Respondent/father,
not appearing, found in default

L.
Kramil-Marcus, Counsel for the child, C. N.

M.
LaFrance, Counsel for the child, T. N.

E N D O R S E M E N T

[
1
]

The dominant philosophy of child protection law is that the state should
only intervene as a last resort.  The clear focus of the legislation is the
protection of and well being of children
[1]
.

[
2
]

Diversity of parenting style is welcomed but the right of parents to
raise their children as they see fit is secondary to the right of children to
be safe.  Here, the state through its mandated agency, the Society, correctly intervened.
Much of the focus of this extensive litigation related to the mother’s mental
health but the true focus remains the safety of two children within their
family system. The protection concerns are overwhelming and uncontradicted.

[
3
]

This application is about two children: T., age 16, born March 5, 1991
and C., age 13, born May 29, 1993.  This matter has an extensive history of
litigation.  This is the 25
th
court appearance in almost two years. The
mother is self- represented.  The two children were found to be in need of
protection by a previous order.  This is a disposition hearing only.

[
4
]

The Frontenac Children’s Aid Society (the “Society”) has requested:

(a)

An Order to
strike the respondent mother’s [C.N.] Answer and her documents filed in the
Continuing Record.

(b)

Upon an Order granting
the relief sought above, holding an uncontested trial by affidavit evidence for
a final Order that the child C. born May 29, 1993 be made a ward of the
Frontenac Children’s Aid Society or its designate, the Brantford Children’s Aid
Society, for a period of three months and a final three month supervision order
placing the child, T. born March 5, 1991 in the care of the mother under the
supervision of the Frontenac Children’s Aid Society or its designate, the
Brantford Children’s Aid Society.

(c)

Upon the Order
granting the relief sought in (b), an Order transferring the case to the Ontario
Court of Justice in Brantford.

RESULT

[
5
]

The respondent mother’s Answer is struck but not the affidavits filed by
her.  This matter proceeded by uncontested trial and the relief is granted. The
motion to transfer the case to the Ontario Court of Justice in Brantford is
dismissed.

BACKGROUND

[
6
]

Since 2001, community resources and family members have  reported
protection concerns to the Society.  The Society attempted to work with the
mother, in particular to ensure the children’s school attendance and medical
treatment.   The mother was adamant that this child had a psychiatric disorder.
She inappropriately medicated him.  Medical authorities disagreed with her.

[
7
]

The materials depict the mother with a family history of
abuse and dysfunction.  The adults in her life failed to protect her.  She was
sexually abused by her father.  The mother reports that her own father later
tried to murder her.  She also suspects that her own mother was involved with
her brother’s disappearance and death.  Her material indicated that her father
had put her brother in the oven and turned it on.  She said her father tried to
throw her off a cliff and her mother knew about it.  She also described an
incident where her father went after her mother with an axe and that she
witnessed her mother falling to the floor as the axe cut into the bathroom door
above her head.  She disclosed horrific events including the attempted
strangling of her sibling and the abuse of pets.  She indicated her father
eventually committed suicide while the police were investigating her father for
trying to murder her.  She received substantial life insurance proceeds upon
his death.  The mother indicates that her own family blamed her for promoting
her father’s suicide and her family tried to get her charged with his murder.  She
reported she was threatened and stalked by a former partner.  While there is
dispute about some of these events, without any doubt, she has led a difficult
life experiencing abuse and violence at the hands of others.  In many respects,
she was robbed of her childhood.

[
8
]

A 2003 psychiatric note diagnoses the mother “on Axis I with a
delusional disorder, manic schizophrenia and on Axis II with anti-social and
borderline paranoid personality traits.”  It described the mother as refusing
to discuss treatment plans such as medication.

[
9
]

Psychologist Elizabeth de Grace wrote in a report dated February 13,
2004 that the mother had “an encapsulated delusional system which includes a
belief that C. has a major psychiatric disorder, schizophrenia.”  In summary, the
doctor noted that all medical professionals have indicated that the child may
have symptoms of an anxiety disorder, not a psychosis.  The doctor went on to
state, “C. is a young man who has specific learning disabilities, but is
otherwise healthy.  He is both highly protective and dependent on his mother.
He is not in a position to be able to act on his own behalf or in his own
welfare.  He is experiencing continuous feedback from his mother that he is
sick.  As a child, he is not equipped to evaluate the information given him
about himself.  He is isolated from alternative adult caregivers who would be
able to support and guide him.  C. may also be afraid because of the paranoid
content of [mother’s] delusional system.  The long-term consequences of living
in this environment will be very serious as he continues to develop.”

[
10
]

A
special education program was organized for this child.  The mother failed to
follow through.  In 2005, the younger child was absent from school 73 days and
was late 29 days. An interim supervision order was granted on May 30, 2005 for
both children.  It was based on concerns regarding extremely poor school
attendance and psychiatric reports which indicated the mother insisted the younger
child was schizophrenic and that she kept him home from school because of his
illness.  Later in that year, on October 18, 2005, the children were admitted
into care in consequence of the mother’s failure to comply with the order.  An
interim care hearing on November 10, 2005 required the children to remain in
care.  The children were found to be in need of protection.

[
11
]

The situation
deteriorated when the mother connected with Canada Court Watch, a
self-appointed interest group.  In the fall of 2005, the older child, T.,
disappeared from the Society’s care and with the mother’s help went to live
with Vernon Beck, a member of the Canada Court Watch group.  This interference
was without the consent of the Society.  It was contrary to the order and
contrary to the interests of the children.

[
12
]

The
mother was directly involved in the disappearance of the child with the
assistance of the Canada Court Watch group.  The Society took significant and
serious steps to try and resolve the issue.  Enforcement proceedings, including
contempt, were brought before the court.

[
13
]

Later,
the child T. was placed in the care of a maternal aunt and the younger child
remained in care.  Further problems occurred.  During a sibling access visit at
the aunt’s home, the older child, T., held a hatchet to the younger child, C’s.,
throat.  When the aunt sought to retrieve the weapon, the elder child, T., ran
from the home.  The police were called.  The placement broke down.

[
14
]

The
older child, T., was then ordered into the Society’s care.  Several motions
addressed access issues. The mother undermined the placements and resisted
orders.    Her access continued to concern the Society and eventually, the
police became involved at the Society’s office.

[
15
]

The younger
child, C., made enormous strides while in care.  His lawyer last saw him July
14, 2006.  At that time, he was excited about his new foster home, had made
friends and was going to school.  While in the care of the Society, the younger
child C. was taken off all medications pursuant to medical advice and successfully
attended a regular full-time education placement.

[
16
]

The
younger child, C., disappeared August 17, 2006 and has not been seen by
authorities in the seven months before this hearing.  There have been, however,
some sightings on the internet by means of a video between the two brothers.
Authorities continue to search for him.  The mother purports to look for him
but her concern about her missing son is disproportionately weak given her intense
love for him.

[
17
]

The
immediate concern is that the mother has taken and hidden the child C.  There
is a worry she has placed him with inappropriate caretakers. The court found on
September 8, 2006 that the mother participated “either directly or indirectly
in the disappearance of C. and knows where C. is.”  In addition, the mother was
found to have directly or indirectly published material in a newspaper or on
the internet, contrary to
section 45(8)
of the
Child and Family Services Act
,
R.S.O. 1990, c. C. 11 (the “
CFSA
”)

and contrary to an Order made
March 8, 2006.  The court ordered the mother to return the younger child by a
specific date and to refrain from any further publication with respect to this
matter and to remove from her internet site any material identifying anyone involved
in the protection proceedings.

[
18
]

The
mother failed to do so.  In consequence of her contempt, she was punished by incarceration
for thirty days in the fall of 2006.

[
19
]

The
protection concerns became exacerbated.  The relationship between the mother and
the Society broke down even further.  The mother publicly expanded websites
which exposed the children to risk.  Several motions and applications dealt
with the issues of publication and enforcement.  The mother meanwhile had relocated
herself to Brantford and purchased a home although she was not previously well connected
to that community. This choice created some geographical issues for her court
attendance, participation in the assessment, access and continuity of service.
The Society tried to implement a creative and realistic plan within the
confines of an impossible power struggle. Eventually, the older child T. was
returned to the care of the mother under a Supervision Order where there can be
token monitoring of his safety by the Brantford Society.  The concerns remained
but the hope was that at least in the mother’s care, he would be in school and
have some community contact.  He would no longer be as the mother described, a
“fugitive”.  I do not criticize the Society for trying this option.

[
20
]

The Brantford
Society reports the mother to be co-operative in the seven months working with
her.  This is positive and beneficial in resolving the outstanding issues.  So
far however, I find the mother has been unchallenged by the Brantford Society to
fulfill the most basic terms of the interim order such as ensuring school
attendance, consultation by T. with his lawyer and some unannounced visits to
the child by authorities.  There was reference to counseling for T. but no
evidence of T.’s actual attendance or participation.  I find the level of supervision
by the Society or its designate to be unsatisfactory and below an acceptable
standard. T. is losing another school year and he cannot afford it. The
supervision order made here must be obeyed.

[
21
]

In
the seven months since the interim supervision order returning T. to the care
of his mother, he has attended only two days at school.  Attending school is
not only a right of a child but an important responsibility of a parent.  The
worker indicated the child missed school on the day she met with him because he
was tired from being up late the previous night.  This is not an acceptable
reason for him not going to school.  There is a vague suggestion about home
schooling which I find doubtful.  The identity and credentials of any home
school teacher and the curriculum followed are unknown.  As a term of
supervision, the Society is required to determine the number of credits that T.
is eligible to receive.  The child T. is not going to school and already has a
history of learning challenges.  The mother knows the need for a formal education. In 2004 she returned to upgrade her education as an adult,
and graduated as a dental assistant.  It is clear on the basis of the
evidence that without an education, both of these children will be sentenced to
a life of poverty.  Time is of the essence to help them.

[
22
]

Paragraph
3(c) of the interim supervision order, specifically required the mother to
facilitate a meeting with T. and his lawyer.  She failed to do this.  The
mother telephoned the child’s lawyer, leaving a message.  That is insufficient.
There is a history of the mother resisting the children’s access to their
lawyers.  He needs legal advice.  His lawyer can help him.

[
23
]

The
initial protection concerns outlined by the Society have been exacerbated into
a heartbreaking catastrophe for the children.  This matter started with
concerns that could have been easily resolved by the mother.  She needed to
adhere to medical advice and make sure the children went to school.  Instead,
it has blown up into a struggle where the mother went to jail and ongoing
contact between C. and his family is in jeopardy.  T. is also at risk as a
result of her influence.  Now that T. is sixteen, the line between his
involvement as a child/victim or active adult participant in hiding the younger
brother is blurry.  The video of the two brothers shows they have contact.  His
alignment with the mother in hiding C. is legally hazardous and draws T. into
the conflict.  The risk now is the potential criminalization of family issues
for the mother and for T.  The mother can fix the problems.

[
24
]

Psychiatric
and professional evidence filed on behalf of the Society including two
assessments have confirmed serious issues about the mother’s mental health and
its negative impact upon the children.  A psychiatric assessment dated December
11, 2006 indicates that the mother confirmed to the assessor the mother’s
belief that the younger child has suffered from schizophrenia in the past.  Both
children, at different times, have disappeared from the care of the Society.  The
mother has been instrumental in their departure.

[
25
]

The
Family Court Clinic Assessment dated January 19, 2007 explained the substantial
and grave impact upon the children of the mother’s pattern of thinking.  The
younger child has been led to believe he is mentally ill.  That child has
aligned with the mother and supports the mother’s perception.  The assessor
stated that the child coped with his bizarre family situation by being highly
compliant, accommodating and adaptable.  She outlined that there was little
opportunity for the child to focus on normal, preadolescent tasks.  With the
child in hiding, the assessor stated that he would likely continue to be loyal
to the mother, even if he were held indefinitely in a hostage situation.  The
child had learned to comply with the mother’s beliefs and actions.  He is at
risk of having and developing distorted beliefs and attitudes that will hamper
his emotional behavior and academic function.  The mother has no insight into
her disorder whatsoever and the progress for change is dismal.   When
challenged, the mother’s demeanor became intense and hostile.  A theme emerged
that she was being persecuted.  The assessor indicated a high risk that the
mother’s mental disorder would have a severe, deleterious affect on the child’s
emotional well being and recommended the child become a Crown ward.

[
26
]

The mother has a history of disputes with police, protection
authorities and the medical community.  She published her complaints on a
website and dedicated another web site to police corruption.  Her demeanor
elevates security levels.  She made several serious complaints against social
workers and police and felt she was victimized and harassed by authorities.  She
has bullied, intimidated, frightened and threatened authorities and others who
disagree with her.  This conduct makes her hard to serve as a client and
dangerous as a parent.

ISSUE 1 – STRIKING OUT
PLEADINGS

[
27
]

The
Family
Law Rules
, O. Reg. 114/99,
Courts of Justice Act
, R.S.O. 1990, c.
C-43 (“
Rules
”)

allow a court to strike out pleadings where a
party fails to follow the rules, obey a court order or where the pleadings set
out have no reasonable claim or defence in law. The protection concerns have
escalated with delay.
Rule 14(23)
states that where a party does not obey an
Order made on motion, in addition to the other remedies, the court may strike
out a party’s Answer or other documents.

[
28
]

Although I strike
out the mother’s Answer, I do not strike out her Affidavit material.  It is an
important addition to the complete record of the court and provides the court
with her viewpoint.  This mother has some community
support such as the Salvation Army supervised access program.  They, for
example, provided a positive account and made some helpful
observations.

[
29
]

I have reviewed the
entire file.  It is voluminous.  Despite the mother’s evidence, I find that
there is compelling, credible, uncontradicted evidence which requires the Order
to be made.

[
30
]

The courts have been reluctant to
extend the power to strike pleadings in child protection matters because it
would foreclose a parent’s ability to assist the court in determining the best
interests of children.  In the circumstances of this case, I find the remedy
appropriate.  The mother is not influenced by court orders and has been found
in contempt and punished.  She still declined to obey the directions of the
court.  She concedes school and health issues.  The relief sought by the
Society is in the best interests of the children.  It is temporary and less
intrusive than the assessment recommendation of crown wardship.

[
31
]

The delay from the initial
application to date is significant.  Tremendous public resources have been
spent in bringing the matter before the court and searching for the children.  The
mother’s actions, including her self representation, have frustrated the
ability for meaningful case management, a negotiated resolution, or a trial on
the substance of the issues.  The
Rules
and case law in child welfare
matters emphasize the necessity to bring finality to disputes involving
children.  Permanency is critical.  Almost two years have lapsed since the
Society brought this application.  I find that any prejudice to the mother in
proceeding to strike her answer and finalize the matter must be balanced by the
prejudice to the children of further delay and an inability to have their
permanency determined.  After almost two years, and twenty five court
appearances, I find that the mother is not inclined to settle or try the issues.
The litigation process itself has in my view negatively affected the
children’s interests.

[
32
]

No purpose of further adjournment
would be served.  The mother has stopped participating.  Despite twenty-five
court appearances of substance, no settlement conference has actually occurred
on the merits despite special arrangements to help her.  She failed to file
material or attend.  The Society arranged transportation for her.  She did not
accept it.  The Society indicates that the mother’s website states she is
boycotting the court.

[
33
]

The record indicates she last
attended the court June 29, 2006 when the assessment was ordered and
arrangements were made for the only appointment between the older child and his
counsel.  She has interfered with her children’s right to counsel.  The younger
child C. is missing and has not attended school.  There is serious risk that
his development is impaired by his social and educational isolation.  A court
has found she is involved with his disappearance.  Resolution is urgent for the
children.  They are losing their childhood.  I find that the Answer of the
mother should be struck and the matter should proceed by summary trial.

ISSUE 2 – SUMMARY JUDGMENT

[
34
]

By
Order of January 24, 2007, the Society was granted leave to bring a motion to
strike the pleadings of the mother and to seek a summary trial.  Since that
time, the mother has not filed material with the court, has not produced the
child or paid the costs ordered.  In this matter, the mother was served with
the affidavit of the Society and chose not to file material, or oppose the
Answer being struck out or to attend court.  Every effort was made to
accommodate the mother to participate in the process.  Rule 16 allows the court
to make an order for summary judgment.

[
35
]

A 13
year old child has been missing for more than seven months.  The Society has
filed evidence that he is not in school and does not have the benefit of a
stable family environment.  The Society is worried about his whereabouts, his
caretakers and that he may be given inappropriate psychiatric medications
again.  No purpose would be served by a lengthy trial. While there are many
issues that could have been tried, the overwhelming protection issues are well
documented and well supported by the evidence of the Society.

[
36
]

The
usual tools available to a court to encourage a party to resolve a matter have
not worked.  In this matter, there has been a finding of contempt and a period
of incarceration.  That did not provide the mother with sufficient incentive to
produce the child.

[
37
]

Rule
10(5) provides that where an Answer is struck out, the respondent is not
entitled to further notice of the steps in the case, or to participate in the
case, and the court may deal with the case in the respondent’s absence.

[
38
]

The burden in summary judgment motions in child protection proceedings
is on the moving party, the Society, to show that there is no triable issue
(see
Children’s Aid Society of Halton Region v. K.L.A.
,
2006 CanLII 33538 (ON CA)
, [2006] O.J. No.
3958 at para.
19
(C.A.)).  The Society has met this burden.

[
39
]

I am mindful of the fact the court’s jurisdiction to grant summary
judgment in child protection proceedings must be exercised with caution (see
Children’s
Aid Society of Halton Region v. K.L.A
. at para.
25
, citing
F.B. v. S.G.

(2001),
2001 CanLII 28231 (ON SC)
, 199 D.L.R. (4th) 554 (Ont. S.C.J.).

[
40
]

I
have specifically reviewed the case law including Children’s Aid Society of
Regional Municipality of Waterloo v. V.L.,
2006 CanLII 32610 (ON SC)
, [2006] O.J. No. 3785 (S.C.J.); R.A.
v. Jewish Family and Child Service,
[2001] O.J. No. 47 (S.C.J.)
; London and
Middlesex v. L.A. and H.C. No. 1,
1999 CanLII 20470 (ON CTGD)
, [1999] O.J. 5839 (Gen. Div.) and Family and
Children Services of Guelph and Wellington County v. E.W.,
[2001] O.J. No. 2279
(C.J.)
.

[
41
]

In
Children’s Aid Society of the Regional Municipality of Waterloo v. V.L.
, the court reviewed the test for summary judgment (at para. 48).  The
court must be satisfied that the test has been met and that the order made will
prevent the children from being held in a litigation limbo.  The CAS must disclose its full case to the court. The court must take a
"good, hard look" at the "full evidentiary record" to
determine if there are any factual issues in dispute which create a genuine
issue for trial (decision of Justice Hardman in
Children's
Aid Society of the Regional Municipality of Waterloo v. R.S.
,
2000 CanLII 22902 (ON CJ)
, [2000] O.J. No. 4880, paras.
22-23
).

[
42
]

I
followed the legislative path as outlined in the
CFSA
and find that the
Order made is in the best interests of both children.

[
43
]

In deciding disposition the court is
required:

(a)

to make its decision based on the
child’s best interests (
CFSA
:
s. 57
)

(b)

to ascertain what efforts have been
made by the Society or another agency or person to assist before intervention (
CFSA
:

s. 57(2)
)

(c)

not to remove the child from the person
who had charge of the child prior to intervention unless the court is satisfied
that alternatives that are “
less disruptive to the child
” would be
inadequate to protect the child. The alternatives include non-residential
services and the assistance referred to in
s. 57 (2)
of the
CFSA
(
CFSA
:

s. 57(3)
)

(d)

t
o consider other community placements (
CFSA
:

s. 57(4)
)

[
44
]

In determining the appropriate order
the court must be aware of time limitations set out within the Act.  In
general, the court cannot make an order for society wardship that results in a
child being a society ward for a period exceeding:

(a)

12 months, if the child is less than 6
years of age on the day the court makes an order for society wardship;

(b)

24 months, if the child is 6 years of
age or older on the day the court makes an order for society wardship (
CFSA
:

s. 70(1)
)

[
45
]

I am
satisfied that the orders as requested are the least intrusive orders
available.  A community placement was tried for T., and failed on account of
the mother’s interference.  I find that there is no community placement that
would allow for a less restrictive plan for the younger child.  There are
significant security problems.  I do note that the Society indicated that a
group placement was available for the child.  The assessor strongly discouraged
a group placement.  I urge the Society to place the child upon his return to
care in the foster home where he flourished or such other family placement that
might best suit his needs so long as security concerns can be adequately
addressed.  While in the foster home environment, he made friends, lost the
weight he gained as a side effect of the drugs, went to school and did well in
their care.

[
46
]

The
current disappearance of the younger child C., previous disappearance of T.,
the failure of both children to have their educational needs met, health issues
and the resulting consequences to the children of their mother’s conduct and
belief system clearly support a finding that their best interests are served by
making the orders as requested by the Society.

[
47
]

I am
satisfied that the Society made reasonable effort to assist the mother and the
children prior to court intervention.  There is a serious risk of
harm to the children without the benefit of a court order.  I further find that
the prognosis for change of the mother in obtaining treatment, and repairing
the problems is bleak.  The statutory time limits are rapidly running out.  I
find that it is a foregone conclusion that without the benefit of a protection
order the children will not, at the minimum, have their health and educational
needs met.  For those concerns, I find there is no genuine issue requiring a
trial.  The motion for summary judgment is granted.

ISSUE 3 – MOTION TO TRANSFER

[
48
]

The
Society also sought an order to transfer the file from Kingston to Brantford
where the mother now resides.  A previous request by the mother to transfer
this matter was also rejected.  There now seems to be consent between the
Society and the mother’s initial claim that the matter be transferred.  Without
the production of the child, I am unprepared to transfer this matter.  Although
the request is unopposed, I find the substantial convenience remains in this
jurisdiction.  I do not find it would be in the child’s best interests to grant
the motion with respect to the child C.  His assessment, medical and special
resources are in Kingston.  His lawyer is Kingston.  The foster home where he
flourished, the school he succeeded in and the friends he made are in the Kingston
area.  The workers who have familiarity with him are in this jurisdiction.  There
is no current order being made for access at this time to the mother or brother
in Brantford.  A transfer of the file while he remains missing would be
counterproductive to his security.  The mother’s failure to cooperate with
authorities and disregard for the legal system would make such a transfer inappropriate
at this time.

[
49
]

When
C. is returned to Society care, then the child through his counsel may renew
the motion.  The motion to transfer the case to Ontario Court of Justice in Brantford
is dismissed.

CONCLUSION

[
50
]

The
child T. shall be placed in the care of the mother subject to an Order for a
three month Supervision Order as requested by the Society.  The primary term
relates to ensuring his educational and counseling needs are met.  He shall be
produced to his lawyer by the mother when requested.

[
51
]

The child C. shall be placed as a ward of the Society until the later of
June 29
th
, 2007 or three months after he is located and returned to
the care of the Society.

[
52
]

In the absence of C., I make no order for access by the mother or T. to
the child. Interim access arrangements were disruptive.  Security issues are
elevated.   His condition is unknown.  The child’s counsel lacks current
instructions because he is missing.  I do note that historically, both children
have always expressed a desire for contact with their mother. She has many fine
qualities.  When C. is located, he will return to the care of the Society.  As
his guardian, the Society may decide to facilitate contact between the children
and others including his brother and mother if appropriate.  The Society does
not need an order for this. To clarify, this means the Society is not required
to facilitate access but not prevented from it either.  Several interim access
orders were tried but unsuccessful.  Visits between C., his brother, T. and the
mother will depend upon the mother’s willingness to co-operate and the child’s
circumstances after he is returned.  Currently, T. is aligned with his mother.  Sadly,
I find that an order requiring access between the children is not in C.’s best
interests at this time.

[
53
]

The
child C., through his counsel, may return the access issue to court if he
requests access to his brother or mother or seeks to renew the motion to
transfer the case to Brantford.  No notice to the mother is needed on the issue
of access or the transfer to Brantford because those two issues were considered
in this decision and have already been determined in relation to her.  C.’s
viewpoint was not properly before the court because he was missing and his
lawyer had no instructions.  I would like to hear from him through his lawyer.  If
T. instructs his lawyer that he was unaware of his right to consult his lawyer,
he may also return to court on the issue of access to C. after he is recovered.

[
54
]

Although
the parties are in the midst of a serious conflict, all of the relevant people
who have encountered these children, whether within the mother’s system or the
protection authorities, have been affected by the boys’ compelling
personalities.  I find the mother loves her children.  I ask her to step back
and review her options for a successful outcome.  These two boys require the
benefit of a negotiated solution.  I urge her to choose a path of resolution
for their sake, regardless of her viewpoint, that will maximize their opportunities
for a peaceful life and minimize further conflict.  The first step in that
process is the production of C.

ENDORSEMENT

(i)

The respondent mother’s Answer is struck but not
the affidavits filed by her.

(ii)

This matter proceeded by uncontested trial.

(iii)

The child C. born May 29, 1993 be made a ward of
the Frontenac Children’s Aid Society until the later of June 29
th
,
2007 or  three months after he is located and returned to the care of the
Society. There is no order for access by the mother or T. to the child.

(iv)

The child, T. born March 5, 1991 shall be placed
in the care of the mother under the supervision of the Frontenac Children’s Aid
Society or its designate, the Brantford Children’s Aid Society  for a period of
three months, on the following terms and conditions:

a.

The mother and T. will work cooperatively with
the Society and other community service providers as deemed necessary by the
Society.

b.

T. will  attend any counselling or any support
services recommended by the Society.

c.

The mother will cause T. to meet with his
lawyer, Mark LaFrance and will facilitate T. meeting Society designated
representatives, support services, counsellors, school officials or any one
else deemed necessary by the Society.

d.

The mother will permit the Society access to the
child T. on an announced and unannounced basis at home, in the community and at
school.

e.

T. will attend school on a regular basis.  The
mother will cause the child to attend school.  Society or its representative
will have access to T. at school and to his school records to ensure he is
attending and actively participating in  his classes.

f.

The mother will sign consent forms permitting
open disclosure between all relevant service providers.

g.

The mother will notify the Society immediately of
any contact, direct or indirect,  she has with the child C. This includes any
knowledge she has of contact between T. andC.

h.

The mother will notify the Society within 24
hours of any significant changes to her personal circumstance including, but
not limited to:  change of address or change of phone number.

i.

The Society or its designate,  shall
determine the  educational status of T. including  his current completed  number
of high  school credits.  If the child is home schooled, the Society is to
determine the identity and credentials of the teacher and the curriculum being
followed.

(v)

The motion to transfer the case to the Ontario
Court of Justice in Brantford
is dismissed.

1.(1) The paramount purpose of this Act is to promote
the best interests, protection and well being of children.

(2)  The additional purposes of this Act, so long as they are consistent with
the best interests, protection and well being of children, are:

1.

To recognize that while parents
may need help in caring for their children, that help should give support to
the autonomy and integrity of the family unit and, wherever possible, be
provided on the basis of mutual consent.

2.

To recognize that the least
disruptive course of action that is available and is appropriate in a
particular case to help a child should be considered.

3.

To recognize that children’s
services should be provided in a manner that,

i.

respects a child’s need for
continuity of care and for stable relationships within a family and cultural
environment,

ii.

takes into account physical,
cultural, emotional, spiritual, mental and developmental needs and differences
among children,

iii.

provides early assessment,
planning and decision-making to achieve permanent plans for children in
accordance with their best interests, and

iv.

includes the participation of a
child, his or her parents and relatives and the members of the child’s extended
family and community, where appropriate.
